title: Insecticide toxicity load tripled on US bird survey routes in 1992-2014, but it explained only about 1% (at most 3%) of the gap between bird community warming and climate warming
abstract: Question: did agricultural insecticides, a pollutant whose toxic load increased strongly, decrease warm-adapted birds and so hide part of the climate response of the bird community temperature index (CTI)? Data: 50,367 standard North American Breeding Bird Survey runs on 3,463 contiguous-US routes in 1992-2014; USGS EPest county pesticide estimates; honey-bee LD50 values of 82 insecticides (DiBartolo et al. 2019) to calculate the acute insecticide toxicity load (AITL) on route footprints; GHCN_CAMS May-July temperature. Method: within-route models with route x observer and year effects; a trend budget that compares the observed CTI trend with the spatial-slope expectation, with 400 state-block bootstraps; Poisson models for 294 species. Results: the route AITL increased about three times (89% from neonicotinoids in 2014). The CTI changed by -0.006 C per log unit of AITL (state-clustered SE 0.005); lag, lead, mass-based, EPest-low and BCR x year variants were also small. The expected CTI trend was 0.190 C per decade and the observed trend 0.041 C per decade. The pesticide part was -0.0015 C per decade, 1.0% of the gap (95% CI -0.4% to 3.0%); on the most exposed third of routes it was 3.4% (upper limit about 10%). Species did not show a general pesticide decline (17 negative and 40 positive significant slopes); slopes decreased only weakly with species temperature index (-0.12 points per C), and the species-implied CTI response (-0.005) agreed with the route estimate. Route-mean exposure did not change the spatial slope (0.453 to 0.446). Conclusion: insecticide pollution does not set the bird climate-tracking gap, because pesticide sensitivity is almost unrelated to thermal niche. Limitations: correlational design, a non-zero lead placebo, county-level exposure estimates, bee-based toxicity weights, no data after 2014.
